rationale: B wins because it has the nerve to turn the dangerous facts into actual stories, especially "Toast doesn't say how often its restaurant cash advances go bad." A is strong, but it parks one of the best conflicts in the refuse pile: "Toast responds to fee criticism" as a mere standing vulnerability. That is too polite; the fee tension becomes more newsworthy when Toast bundles more financial products into the same operator relationship.
gaps_in_A: "Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware" asserts causality the update does not give. Higher-margin fintech plus recent profitability is not proof that lending caused profitability.
"Toast responds to fee criticism" defensive-comment is refused too aggressively. The bundling news gives fee complaints a live operator-economics hook.
"underwritten by the payment flow Toast already sees" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts. Treat it as a proof question, not a stated premise.
"tip pooling, wage credits, variable shifts" adds plausible restaurant-payroll texture beyond the update. The set partly catches itself, but the angle still leans on unsupported specifics.
gaps_in_B: "Toast's profits are coming from lending and payroll, not the point-of-sale hardware it's known for" overclaims. The update says fintech is higher-margin, not that payroll and lending produced the profit.
"a lender wearing a software company's branding" is a sharp line that outruns the evidence. Toast Capital cash advances do not by themselves make Toast essentially a lender.
"paid financial products" assumes the bundled lending and payroll products add operator fees. Likely, but not supplied; the angle needs pricing proof before pitch.
"Toast just disclosed" adds a disclosure shape without a source or timestamp. The set wisely asks later where the update originated, but the angle should not pretend that is already known.
